title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
content:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.
Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”
One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”
In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.
Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

report.summary: Anthropic reports fewer junior technical hires and more meeting time as Claude reshapes its workforce, offering a preview of AI-driven organizational change.
report.background: Anthropic is an AI lab behind Claude and has deliberately rebuilt its workflows around AI tools. In an October 2026 report, it says its internal workforce trends may signal how AI could affect hiring, work organization, and labor demand across the economy. The report arrives as companies debate whether AI coding agents reduce the need for entry-level engineers, increase productivity, or simply shift work toward oversight and coordination. While Anthropic cautions that other organizations may not adopt AI as deeply, its data offers one of the clearest public looks at how an AI-native company is changing internally.
key_points: Junior representation in technical departments fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025, while the share of junior technical hires dropped more sharply from 27% to 9%. The company is clearly hiring fewer entry-level technical workers as AI takes on more routine tasks.

Technical teams now make up 56% of Anthropic’s workforce, down from 61%. Anthropic attributes this partly to normal business expansion and partly to coding tools letting non-technical employees build software themselves.

Employees report productivity gains but also a shift toward managing AI. In an April 2026 survey, 27% said Claude made them more productive and 20% said their job moved from doing work to managing Claudes, creating new attention demands.

Meeting time per employee rose 20% year over year and 16% for technical contributors. Anthropic links this to the continued need for human trust, accountability, and face-to-face coordination rather than purely asynchronous AI work.

Anthropic cites more code per person, more sales per representative, and more contracts processed. It acknowledges that more code does not guarantee better code or business impact, but says it has not found signs of declining code quality.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic’s report is a notable data point in the debate over AI’s labor effects: productivity can rise while entry-level hiring shrinks and coordination costs grow. It suggests agentic coding tools may compress routine technical work but increase demand for review, judgment, and management. For developers, the emphasis shifts toward orchestrating AI agents, reviewing generated output, and communicating across teams rather than only writing code. For regular users, the report hints at a future with more AI-generated work to verify and more human coordination to establish trust. It also raises concerns about how junior talent will build skills if entry-level roles become scarcer.
report.tools: To follow these shifts, watch Anthropic’s Economic Index and future workplace reports, and try Claude Code for agentic software development. Open-source orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI are useful for studying how teams manage multiple AI agents. Workflow and collaboration analytics tools can help organizations measure meeting load and review bottlenecks, though no single tool directly replicates Anthropic’s internal analysis.
